articles.title_orig: China's industrial strength benefits global growth
articles.title_zh: China's industrial strength benefits global growth
articles.content_orig:
By MA SI in Shenzhen, Guangdong | 
          China Daily |
          Updated: 2026-11-23 07:26
China's manufacturing prowess is not "stealing jobs" from the rest of the world but creating shared opportunities through localized production, technology transfers and complementary trade, business leaders and experts said.
They made the comments during the 2026 APEC Economic Leaders' Week in Shenzhen, Guangdong province, pushing back against the so-called "China Shock 2.0" narrative that portrays the country's industrial rise as a zero-sum threat to global employment.
Wang Chuanfu, chairman and president of Chinese electric vehicle maker BYD, said many people outside China have some misconceptions about the country's manufacturing capabilities.
Citing BYD's operations in Chile, Wang said the company purchases large quantities of copper and lithium there and supplies Chinese electric buses that help improve the local environment.
"Our trade is complementary," he said. "We not only export Chinese technology to the world but also bring jobs and tax revenue to local communities, achieving mutually beneficial cooperation and win-win outcomes."
He said that the company's plant in Thailand, with an annual production capacity of 150,000 new energy vehicles, employs nearly 6,000 workers, more than 95 percent of them Thai. He added that most components are sourced locally. Similar arrangements exist at BYD's plants in Indonesia and Brazil.
"We work with 12,000 suppliers globally and aim to benefit the world with Chinese technology through local procurement and research and development," Wang said.
Lei Jun, CEO and chairman of Xiaomi, said, "Asia-Pacific economies form the world's core industrial and supply chain region and the most promising consumer market with strong complementarity and cooperation potential despite their differences."
The company's cars and smartphones require thousands of components, which can only be completed through global supply chain collaboration, he said. "Xiaomi cars will officially enter overseas markets next year," Lei added.
Noting that the automotive industry is a pillar industry in many countries, Lei said cooperating with local supply chains will enable products to better serve local consumers. "We will maintain an open mindset and deepen cooperation with local enterprises," he said.
The European market, including Germany, is among Xiaomi cars' overseas destinations in 2027, and the automaker has already signed memorandums of understanding with eight leading German automotive dealer groups.
Wang Zhisheng, vice-president of the China Chamber of Commerce to the EU, said: "Chinese companies are well aware of the importance of localization — moving from selling cars to Europe to building cars in Europe. We are creating abundant job opportunities for local communities."
BYD's Hungarian plant is set to begin mass production in the fourth quarter of 2026.
Liu Jincheng, founder and chairman of EVE Energy, a major Chinese lithium battery maker, said reaching consensus and co-construction are key aspects of Chinese companies going global.
EVE Energy has built a lithium battery plant in Malaysia and begun nickel resource operations in Indonesia, with nickel already in use in large quantities in luxury cars such as BMW. Its full-industry-chain project in Indonesia will bring electricity to more islands and villages, Liu said.
Li Jiaying, an associate research fellow at Renmin University of China's Chongyang Institute for Financial Studies, said China's real economy is not a source of crisis, but a pillar of global stability.
Describing the so-called "China Shock 2.0" as a deliberately crafted political narrative, Li said that it represents a self-preservation strategy adopted by certain countries confronting industrial disadvantages and domestic deindustrialization. Such countries employ public opinion smears and trade barriers to divert attention from their internal pressures.
Jostein Hauge, a political economist at the University of Cambridge, said the "China Shock 2.0" narrative is steeped in double standards and hegemonic anxiety, while intentionally understating the vast benefits that China's integration into the global economy has delivered to the world.

articles.title_orig: Equipment outage in Atlanta causes over 1,600 Delta flight delays - ABC News
articles.title_zh: Equipment outage in Atlanta causes over 1,600 Delta flight delays - ABC News
articles.source: Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.content_orig:
The delays were not the result of a systems hack, Delta said.
More than 1,600 Delta Air Lines flights nationwide were delayed on Sunday due to a technical issue causing an outage to one of the airline's weight and balance systems, according to Delta.
The equipment snafu comes as millions of people prepare to travel this week for the Thanksgiving holiday, and just days after the Federal Aviation Administration issued the second nationwide ground stop since the 9/11 terrorist attacks due to an equipment installation problem that caused telecommunications issues.
"These delays are not related to any FAA air traffic systems," the FAA said on Sunday about Delta's flight delays.
Delta said later Sunday afternoon that the weight and balance systems had returned to normal operation, and that the outage was not the result of a computer hack.
"Delta is rebooking customers to the next best itinerary and providing meals and hotel rooms where necessary," the airline said. "For customers facing a canceled flight and don’t wish to travel, refunds are being given."
Some 49% of all Delta flights Sunday were delayed by more than 15 minutes, Delta said, after the airline experienced an outage in a system used to calculate the weight and balance of departing flights, Delta said.
The majority of the delayed flights were at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport, but the equipment issue also affected flights to Atlanta from other airports, Delta said.
"Delta teams are using manual workarounds this morning to safely get flights departed while work continues to restore automation. We thank our customers for their patience and our people for their professionalism," Delta said in a statement earlier Sunday.

articles.title_orig: US targets AI chip exports to China, impacting Southeast Asia cloud firms
articles.title_zh: US targets AI chip exports to China, impacting Southeast Asia cloud firms
articles.content_orig:
Trump says he won't allow American companies to build data centres "outside" the US
Donald Trump has said he will ban US companies from building AI data centres overseas, threatening a "tremendous tax" for tech firms who do so.
"We're going to keep it all in this country," the US president said, while providing little detail on the potential policy he said others in his cabinet were hearing about for the first time.
Data centres were a central issue in the midterm elections earlier in November, with many Democratic candidates promising tougher regulation on their construction.
Tech giants including Meta and Google have entered agreements to build data centres overseas. It remains unclear how such a policy would be enforced if it was brought in.
"We're not going to allow our companies to build data centres outside of our country," Trump told reporters in a press briefing following his return from his trip to Asia.
"Because China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen."
But whether that idea will become policy remains unclear.
"I don't know if that's a breaking story, but I haven't even said that to my people. But I'm telling them now, they're here," he said.
Trump floated the policy after saying the US was leading on data centre construction, and he would not allow China to beat the US when it came to AI - which he calls super intelligence, or SI.
It also follows an announcement earlier this week that would restrict the export of advanced computer chips and who can access the computing power provided by them.
Washington on Monday announced firms would require a licence to buy advanced chips, so US officials can monitor whether they are being used to serve Chinese companies or they are being smuggled into China.
The move will impact South East Asian countries that have invested heavily in data centres, as Chinese companies seek to rent computing power from overseas.
Why Canada is embracing AI data centres while the US pushes back
Data centres are crucial to the AI boom. The vast warehouse-style buildings house the advanced computer chips and servers that are needed to run AI programmes such as Claude and ChatGPT.
As of April there were about 3,000 data centres across the US, with another 1,500 in various stages of approval and construction, according to the Pew Research Centre.
Many of them are built in rural areas, and concerns about issues including noise pollution and energy consumption helped drive Democratic candidates promising tougher rules on data centre construction to wins on 3 November.
"You ought to take advantage of the data centres. Make them pay you, make them pay your community, but take advantage don't shut them off," Trump said.
"We have a lot of places that want them badly, and they're great places. They have energy and they have everything. They're tremendous assets."
Large tech firms - often called AI hyperscalers due to the size of their investments in AI - have also been branching out, and Canada has made moves to step in to offer itself as an alternative location for these sites, with less local pushback against projects so far.
Meta has already broken ground on a data centre , external in the province of Alberta, and Anthropic has signed a long-term agreement to lease a proposed data centre in Nova Scotia.
The BBC has reached out to Meta for comment on Trump's remarks.
In September Google announced a â¬13bn ($15bn: Â£11bn) investment in AI infrastructure in Finland, which included funding for three data centres.
Last month, building work for two of those centres was halted due to concerns over the clearance of more than 300 hectares of forest.
Trump called out the build in Finland specifically, saying his administration was "not allowing that to happen".
Google has been contacted for comment.

articles.title_orig: U.S. trade chief sees progress in Canada talks, raises China concerns
articles.title_zh: U.S. trade chief sees progress in Canada talks, raises China concerns
articles.content_orig:
Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney shakes hands with China's President Xi Jinping at the APEC summit on Nov. 19, 2026.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney is placing particular focus on renewing relations with China as he aims to deepen international trade ties and diversify from U.S. reliance amid a three-month-long trade war with the U.S.
When asked what cards Canada holds in its ongoing talks with Washington, Carney, who recently announced a new partnership with the E.U. , pointed to the country's budding relationships elsewhere.
“Our cards are that everyone else in the world wants to deal with us,” he said Wednesday during a remote interview with the New York Times from Shenzhen, China, where he was among the world leaders attending the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit . "If the U.S. doesn't want to do the deal, we're busy.” His remarks came in the wake of President Donald Trump's claim that the U.S. holds “all the cards” after trade talks collapsed in August, leading to both sides enforcing heavy retaliatory tariffs .
Carney and Trump had a meeting on the sidelines of APEC, but aside from a commitment to “continue” negotiations and stay in close contact, no progress was made. However, Carney painted his meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping in a much more positive light. Ahead of the summit, Carney and Xi announced a Canada-China trade pact , which provided additional tariff relief on Canadian food and agricultural exports into China, and in return saw Canada agree to extend tariff exemptions for certain Chinese steel and aluminum products by two years.
Carney, who is promoting a “Canada Strong” platform as he aims to build economic resilience at home, touted the expansion of the trade arrangement with China as something that will deliver “greater certainty and prosperity for all Canadians.” He also praised the negotiation process with China, saying: “They’re very professional. They move forward in a very linear fashion.”
In an eight-day tour that took him from a European summit in Ireland to the Philippines, Cambodia, and finally China for the APEC gathering, Carney forged ahead with his plan to diversify Canada's economy away from its dependence on the U.S., which by far remains the country's largest trading partner .
Experts say Canada's progress in deepening its economic relationships with China could challenge Trump's insistence that Washington holds the upper hand in trade negotiations.
“Part of the Trump Administration’s [belief] is that everybody needs the U.S. more than anything else, and therefore the U.S. has maximum leverage,” says Jennifer Hillman, co-director of the Institute of International Economic Law at Georgetown University. “What this is clearly saying is that Canada can afford to be less willing to give the U.S. whatever it asks for [in negotiations], because they have other options.”
China has the world's second-largest economy , behind only the U.S., giving it the potential to become a much larger market for Canadian goods than some of the other countries Carney has sought to deepen relations with.
“China represents a very big market and the potential of a really big trading partner,” says Lori Turnbull, a professor in the Faculty of Management at Dalhousie University, noting it could be a leverage point in U.S. negotiations. “Doing a deal with a country like China is something that [the U.S.] will care about because of the size of China's economy and its competitive relationship with the U.S.”
Carney's latest push to strengthen trade ties with Beijing forms part of a months-long effort to renew Canada-China relations. In January, he met with Xi to forge what he called a “ new strategic partnership ,” agreeing to allow in up to 49,000 Chinese electric vehicles at a tariff of 6.1%, rather than the previous 100% levy. China agreed to lower tariffs on Canadian agricultural products, including canola seeds, a major Canadian export.
The move drew criticism from Trump, who said that “China will eat Canada alive, completely devour it, including the destruction of their businesses, social fabric, and general way of life.”
While Canada's closer relationship with China could strengthen its hand in negotiations, experts also warn that it could backfire.
Turnbull points to the latest agreement to extend tariff exemptions on Chinese steel and aluminum as a potential source of tension with Washington. “Things like reducing tariffs on select steel and aluminum products coming from China is something that might make the U.S. and not just Donald Trump, but also [U.S. Trade Representative] Jamieson Greer angry,” she suggests.
Steel, aluminum, and auto tariffs were among the major points of contention when U.S.-Canada trade negotiations broke down in August, with both sides accusing each other of walking back commitments.
Carney, however, has played down concerns that Canada's growing trade relationship with China is a major issue for Trump.
“In my conversation with the President, he’s tried to understand where we are with China, where we’re going with China,” said Carney during a news conference in Shenzhen. “I shouldn’t speak for him, but in his hierarchy of issues, it’s not the top issue at all.”
Meanwhile, some Canadian officials have voiced concerns on expanding trade with China.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford warned Carney on Monday against opening the door for more Chinese-made EV vehicles in Canada, arguing the “government’s focus needs to be on protecting Canadian auto workers, not undermining them by importing even more state-subsidized cheap Chinese cars.”
Michael Chong, a lawmaker from Canada’s Conservative Party, during a press conference on Wednesday supported maintaining a dialogue with Beijing, but described Carney’s budding strategic partnership with China as a “risky gambit,” citing potential “national security” concerns.
In 2025, Ottawa identified China as one of the main perpetrators of foreign interference and espionage against Canada alongside other countries such as Russia and Iran. The Canadian government’s own analysis of Canada-China relations also points out that there are "associated risks” in broader trade cooperation in key areas, such as “prevalent and persistent intellectual property theft, and the risk of diversion of sensitive goods and technologies intended for civilian use for military purposes and applications.”
Carney said ahead of his Asia trip that he would raise concerns about foreign interference in his meeting with Xi. "The advantage of these meetings is you can raise issues directly and frankly,” he told reporters in Montreal on Nov. 10. Carney added that he would stress the importance Canada places on "the non-interference in our affairs by China and other countries.”
In a press briefing during the APEC summit, Carney emphasized that Canada's trade with China is largely focused on commodities, rather than sensitive technologies such as advanced semiconductors.
“We are exporting canola, we are exporting pork. We are exporting halibut,” Carney said , also citing liquefied natural gas and oil. “These are important industries. These are not cutting-edge semi-conductors.”
Experts point out that Canada could pursue deeper cooperation with other international partners in sectors where a closer relationship with China would be more difficult, including defense and advanced technology.
“[Canada] is not going to partner with China on defense, security, AI, and digital technology, things like that would be very difficult. [Carney] would have an impossible time trying to convince Canadians that's what we should be doing,” says Turnbull. “For those things, [Canada] would be putting [its] arms around the European Union.”
In September, the European Union unveiled its vision for Canada to become an “associate member” of the bloc. During an E.U.-Canada summit in Montreal in October, the two sides underscored their commitment to this plan, paving the way for deeper cooperation in areas including A

articles.title_orig: Netanyahu’s Likud, Eisenkot’s Yashar end coalition talks without deal
articles.title_zh: Netanyahu’s Likud, Eisenkot’s Yashar end coalition talks without deal
articles.content_orig:
Talks between the parties of caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot to form a unity government have ended without a deal.
Representatives of Netanyahu’s Likud and Eisenkot’s Yashar parties met in a Herzliya hotel on Sunday, where they remained split on who would lead the next government and whether far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir would be part of it, according to Israel’s Channel 12 broadcaster.
The Yedioth Ahronoth newspaper reported that Likud wanted Ben-Gvir in government, while Yashar insisted on his exclusion.
In a joint statement, the two parties said they had “outlined their positions on a range of substantive issues” and that a “follow-up meeting would be held”, without revealing a date or any further details.
Eisenkot has until December 6 to form a government, with the possibility of a 14-day extension, after the elections in October gave his bloc 48 seats – 13 short of a majority.
Netanyahu has called for a unity government , saying it was the only way that Israel’s security could be guaranteed. Such an arrangement would allow a government to be formed without the inclusion of parties led by Palestinian citizens of Israel, which won a record 19 seats.
Channel 12 reported that former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett, who leads the Together list, proposed a coalition of Together, Yashar, Likud and Avigdor Lieberman’s Yisrael Beiteinu, with Eisenkot serving first and Netanyahu succeeding him.
However, Eisenkot has opposed a rotation, and Netanyahu has reportedly insisted on taking the premiership first, while Lieberman has ruled out joining any government that includes Netanyahu altogether.
If unity talks fail, Yashar plans to seek a confidence vote in the Knesset for a minority government before Eisenkot’s mandate expires. It would rely on outside support from the Arab Joint List, led by Yousef Jabareen, and the United Arab List, led by Mansour Abbas.

articles.title_orig: This Is Why Even the Strongmen Are Sick of Trump: Historian
articles.title_zh: This Is Why Even the Strongmen Are Sick of Trump: Historian
articles.content_orig:
By clicking â SIGN UP â you agree to our Terms of Use and Privacy Policy .
Dictators around the globe, some of whom President Donald Trump says heâs âfallen in loveâ with, are growing fed up with the president over his chaotic leadership, a historian revealed.
Speaking on The Daily Beast Podcast , author Simon Sebag Montefiore said that Trumpâs relationships with various autocrats are less about genuine personal affection and more about his awe for their immense power over their countries.
He noted that while Trump has still shown affection for autocratic leaders like Russiaâs Vladimir Putin, Chinaâs Xi Jinping, and leaders in Arab countries, it hasnât been completely reciprocated back in his second term.
Photo Illustration by Victoria Sunday/The Daily Beast/Getty Images
âObviously they have some sort of affinity and, we donât know the details of what it is. I suspect itâs less, letâs say, romantic and exciting than many people like to think. By which I mean, I donât think itâs a meeting of the minds. I donât think it has much warmth or passion âat least from Putinâs side,â Montefiore explained.
âI suspect that when the Russians look at Donald Trump, and Iâm sure this is also true of the Chinese, and I know this is true in the Arab worldâ¦ but I think all of them, youâd have thought that theyâd all be thrilled by the election of Trump, and in some ways they are. But the one thing all these people hate really is spreading disorder, because that can also encompass them and overwhelm them,â he continued.
The White House did not immediately respond to the Daily Beastâs request for comment.
Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping, and U.S. President Donald Trump held a trilateral meeting in China last week.
Montefiore explained to host Joanna Coles that many of these leaders, namely Xi and Putin, are very weary of the disorder and chaos that they have experienced growing up and as young men, so they are uneased by the chaotic leadership style that Trump displays.
âIf I was to put on my hat as an amateur psychologist, I would say that, you know, Trump grew up, you know, admiring powerful people, worshiping powerful people and aspiring to that power,â he explained, adding âhe talked the language of mafia bosses, but, you know, the real mafia bosses are the leaders of autocracies where they really can order people to be whacked when they want.
âSo in some ways, you know, Trumpâs attraction to people like Kim Jong-un and Xi and Putin is that sort of almost boyish admiration for raw power,â he continued.
He added a counterpoint, saying that âon the other hand also, think that they, know, Putin and people like Xi and Putin, and again, the monarchs in the Arab world and dictators in the Arab world are quite alarmed by Putin, quite alarmed by Trump, and they hate unpredictability and they hate erratic decision-making.â
Autocrats like Saudi Crown Prince and Prime Minister Mohammed bin Salman don't like Trump's erratic leadership style.
Jessica Koscielniak/REUTERS
âSo, initially when he came to power, the view in the Arab world was, surprisingly, this man is wild, is extremely pro-Israel,â he continued.
But he said the Arab world realized that this âcould suit us because weâre exhausted with the hypocrisy of American, traditional American leaders who are equally, in some ways, hard to handle.
âAfter all, they say one thing and do another, and this might be easier for us to do business with,â he elaborated.
He went on, âAnd it looked like that in Trump one. In Trump two, I think theyâve walked back that to find Trump a worry and an alarm. And I know that their general attitude is like, they just wanna get through this intact somehow with all the erratic twists and turns.â

articles.title_orig: I stopped talking to my husband and let AI do it instead. He didn’t even notice | Polly Hudson
articles.title_zh: I stopped talking to my husband and let AI do it instead. He didn’t even notice | Polly Hudson
articles.content_orig:
iOS 27 gives the Messages app a variety of welcome upgrades , including one I’ve found myself using a lot: a Smart Reply feature that’s now personalized to the user’s writing style.
When the first wave of Apple Intelligence features were announced in 2024, one that I immediately thought sounded useful was Smart Reply.
The idea behind Smart Reply is simple. Rather than needing to manually type out replies in Messages and Mail, your iPhone can offer prewritten replies you can choose and send with a couple taps.
Great in theory, but the ‘Smart’ part of Smart Reply struggled to materialize in iOS 18.
Fortunately, with a key Apple Intelligence upgrade in iOS 27, the new version of the feature finally lives up to its name. Per Apple :
Smart Reply in Mail and Messages can now draw on a user’s personalized writing style.
Before, Smart Reply would look at the context of a conversation to craft its suggestions. But now, it also aims to match your writing style, punctuation, and tone.
In iOS 18, I almost never used Smart Reply. That’s because despite being fine at suggesting replies that technically worked, those suggestions didn’t sound like me at all.
That’s changed in iOS 27. Smart Reply now consistently impresses me. It no longer offers generic responses that sound like AI wrote them. Instead, its suggestions actually fit with my normal style of communication.
The only drawback is that right now, you’ll only ever see two Smart Reply suggestions. If Apple expanded the feature by letting you scroll horizontally through more options, I suspect I’d use Smart Reply even more.
Have you been using iOS 27’s Smart Reply feature in Messages? Let us know in the comments.

articles.title_orig: Ferrari's New 296 Challenge Stradale Is A 670-HP Race Car You Can Drive Home
articles.title_zh: Ferrari's New 296 Challenge Stradale Is A 670-HP Race Car You Can Drive Home
articles.content_orig:
The curtains open, and for a moment, you're completely transfixed. You know right away that you're looking at something special. This car represents a turning point for Ferrari, a significant departure from what came before. It's a genuine race car that's still somehow legal to drive on the street.
"This is a disruption of balance," says one of the people most closely involved in bringing the car to life. It's easy to see what he means. Even standing still, the Ferrari 296 Challenge Stradale looks like a car built with one thing in mind: setting lap times.
Ferrari even calls it "the production car with the closest connection to a competition vehicle."
No hybrid system. 670 horsepower. Just 2,932 pounds. And 1,360 pounds of downforce at 155 miles per hour. The car was developed alongside the 296 Challenge Evo , which will compete in Ferrari's one-make racing series starting in 2027. The price? Around $307,000.
Ferrari 296 Challenge Stradale
"It's a physical car, fundamentally different to drive. It's not like the 296 Speciale , which is easier and more immediate." Those two sentences tell you almost everything you need to know.
The Speciale is incredibly fast, but it's also approachable. Its electric motor helps with corner exits, drifting, and straight-line acceleration. The Challenge Stradale does away with all of that. There's no hybrid system and no electric motor to fill in the gaps. It's a raw, uncompromising machine with a narrower margin for error, one that relies on aerodynamics to do much of the heavy lifting.
The connection between Ferrari's road cars and its racing program goes back to the company's roots. Enzo Ferrari lived for competition, and in the early days, building road cars was largely a way to fund his racing ambitions. That relationship continues today through the Ferrari Challenge, a customer racing series that has been running since 1993.
It started with the 348, followed by the F355, 360, and every generation since. The 296 Challenge Stradale brings that racing DNA closer to the road than any production Ferrari before it.
Under the hood is the familiar twin-turbocharged 3.0-liter V6 from the 296, with both turbochargers mounted inside the V. The difference is that it now works entirely on its own, producing:
For comparison, the competition-focused 296 Challenge Evo produces 700 hp.
The turbochargers are carried over from the 296 Challenge, as are the thermal barriers. Ferrari focused its development work on boost pressure, variable valve timing, and insulation. The result is a dynamic torque increase of more than 32 percent compared to the 296 GTB. Without an electric motor smoothing things out, throttle response is also much sharper.
The eight-speed dual-clutch transmission has two distinct personalities. Push the car hard, and it switches to the aggressive shifting logic from the 296 Challenge, delivering gear changes in around 170 milliseconds. At lower speeds, it adopts a smoother calibration borrowed from the SF90 XX Stradale. The exhaust note builds all the way to 8,500 rpm, exiting through twin tailpipes derived from the race car.
Performance is predictably serious. The 296 Challenge Stradale hits 60 mph in 2.8 seconds, reaches 124 mph in 7.9 seconds, and tops out at more than 186 mph. Around Ferrari's Fiorano test track, it completes a lap in 1 minute and 18.5 seconds.
The dry weight is just 2,932 pounds with optional equipment, making it 308 pounds lighter than the 296 GTB. That's also the same figure as the 296 Challenge Evo. The result is a power-to-weight ratio of 4.37 pounds per horsepower.
A big part of the weight savings comes from removing the battery and electric motor. Ferrari also fitted a dedicated transmission with a lighter shaft and casing. Then there's the carbon fiber, which appears throughout the car:
For the first time on a production Ferrari, buyers can also request removable seat coverings, leaving parts of the underlying structure exposed.
One figure says a lot about how the Challenge Stradale behaves through corners: body roll is down 68 percent compared to the 296 GTB. Lateral performance improves by 7 percent, while stability increases by 34 percent.
The springs are roughly twice as stiff, requiring an additional spring mounted in series with the main one. It's a setup borrowed directly from the 296 Challenge Evo. The semi-active dampers also get two additional rebound settings, allowing Ferrari to retain at least some compliance when driving on public roads.
The car rides on Pirelli P Zero R tires, with semi-slick P Zero Trofeo RS tires available as an option. Both were specifically developed for the car.
With no regenerative braking system to rely on, stopping power comes entirely from the carbon-ceramic brakes. The front discs measure 15.7 x 1.5 inches, while the rear ones measure 15 x 1.3 inches. Ferrari says the car can stop from 124 mph in just 331 feet.
The traction control system is predictive and calibrated specifically for track driving, marking a first for a road-going Ferrari. It's all managed by the FIVE system, derived from the one used in the F80.
The headline aerodynamic figure is 1,360 pounds of downforce at 155 mph, a 72 percent increase over the 296 GTB. Ferrari achieves this through several carefully designed elements:
At the rear, a fixed wing derived from the 296 Challenge Evo generates 595 pounds of downforce on its own. There's one notable difference, though. Unlike the race car, the wing doesn't use a swan-neck mounting design. Instead, its supports attach from underneath to meet road homologation requirements, particularly those in the United States.
Ferrari's Centro Stile, led by Flavio Manzoni, took the clean design of the 296 and gave it a much more aggressive makeover. A technical insert on the hood, a wing suspended between two bumper-mounted "claws" inspired by the Evo, black metal mesh at the rear, and a double-keel diffuser all serve the same purpose. Here, form follows function.
Buyers looking to make their cars stand out can choose from a dedicated livery, three matte-finish wheel options, and even colored tire inserts through Pirelli's Color Edition program.
The Ferrari 296 Challenge Stradale starts at approximately $307,000.

articles.title_orig: Netanyahu rival condemns ‘Jewish terrorism’ after settler attacks on Palestinian villages
articles.title_zh: Netanyahu rival condemns ‘Jewish terrorism’ after settler attacks on Palestinian villages
articles.content_orig:
Dozens of militant Israeli settlers raided communities on Saturday night, setting fire to vehicles and several homes
Arson attacks by militant Israeli settlers on Palestinian villages in the occupied West Bank have caused a political row in Israel, drawing condemnation from Gadi Eisenkot, the opposition leader, who described them as “Jewish terrorism”.
Dozens of settlers raided Palestinian communities overnight on Saturday, setting fire to about a dozen vehicles and several homes and scrawling racist graffiti. At least four communities were attacked. Israeli police said they had launched an investigation with forensic teams.
Photographs from Kafr Malik , near Ramallah, showed one slogan written in Hebrew that read: “This is the first revenge.” Several vehicles and homes had been set alight in the village.
Images from nearby Deir al-Sudan showed vehicles on fire. Palestinian reports said an agricultural building had been set ablaze in Deir Ballut and cars torched in Deir Abu Mashal.
An ⁠inconclusive election last month stripped Benjamin Netanyahu, the prime minister, of his majority. Eisenkot has been asked to form a government, though his prospects seem little better.
“Last night’s arson attacks in Judea and Samaria were acts of Jewish terrorism, in every sense of the term,” Eisenkot said, using the biblical name for the West Bank. “Extremist groups that set fire to vehicles and homes are undermining regional stability, putting lives at risk and doing grave damage to Israel’s national security and foreign relations.”
Referring to the far-right ministers Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, he added: “The actions led by Ben-Gvir and Smotrich in the West Bank have brought the area to the brink of unchecked anarchy.”
Eisenkot, who has been given 28 days to form a government by the president, Isaac Herzog, with a possible 14-day extension, urged the government and security establishment to “use every tool at their disposal – including administrative detention and targeted operations by the Shin Bet – to stop the rioters and impose harsh sanctions on them”.
In an unprecedented rebuke on Sunday, several other members of the Israeli parliament criticised Netanyahu over escalating violence by militant settlers against Palestinians.
Yair Lapid, the leader of Yesh Atid, held Netanyahu’s government responsible for encouraging the attacks. “Jewish terrorism is the product of criminal negligence by the Israeli government,” he said on X, adding that ministers were deliberately encouraging the militant settlers’ violence “through their silence”.
Yair Golan, the leader of the Democrats party, warned of the possibility of a third intifada and described the West Bank as “on the brink of an explosion”.
“Anyone who wants to prevent a third intifada must replace the current government, which provides cover and support for Jewish terrorism and abandons security,” Golan said on X. “Jewish terrorism harms innocent Palestinians and Israeli army soldiers, and pushes Israel toward unprecedented international isolation.”
Noam Tibon, a retired army major general and Knesset member, gave a similar warning. “If Israel does not eliminate Jewish terrorism in the West Bank, it will destroy Israel,” he wrote.
Netanyahu has not yet responded to the accusations.
Australia announced sanctions on Wednesday against three people and four Israeli entities, including a construction company, over their role in the expansion of illegal settlements and human rights abuses against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.
A day earlier the UK imposed sanctions on eight Israeli construction companies involved in building illegal settlements in the West Bank, which the UN regards as Palestinian territory under Israeli occupation since 1967.
Since the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attacks on Israel, there has been a surge of Israeli settlement expansion and violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank. More than 1,100 Palestinians have been killed there by Israeli forces or settlers.
On Tuesday, a 72-year-old Palestinian woman was shot dead in an overnight attack by Israeli militant settlers in a village near Jericho, where the group has recently moved in after taking over several Palestinian homes.

articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump claimed that the war with Iran will end "right after" the midterm elections in the U.S.
President Donald Trump said Sunday that Iran has launched more missiles and drones over the past week than at any point in more than a year, adding that U. S. forces shot them down without any damage and as tensions escalate following the U.S. midterm elections.
In a post on Truth Social, Trump also tied the surge in Iranian attacks to the Nov. 3 midterm elections, when Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress amid voter frustration over the war with Iran and rising fuel costs.
"As everyone remembers, I predicted two things concerning the November 3rd Midterm Elections," Trump wrote on Truth Social.
TRUMP RESPONDS AFTER VANCE BLAMES IRAN WAR FOR MIDTERM LOSSES, VP SAYS HIS JOB IS TO SUPPORT PRESIDENT
President Donald Trump said Iran has launched more missiles and drones over the past week than at any point in more than a year, claiming U.S. forces intercepted them all without damage. (Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images)
"One, that if the Democrats win, the Stock Markets would go down, substantially, which they have, and two, that the Islamic Republic of Iran, which has killed 81,000 protestors as of today, will grow more aggressive in their attacks, which has also occurred. "
Trump also said that Iran launched "more drones and missiles over the past week than at any time for over a year," though he said U.S. defenses neutralized the threat.
"Don't worry, they've all been knocked down, and done no damage," Trump said.
"Iranian leaders consider the Democrats weak, ineffective, and Country destroying, but I won't let that happen!" he added.
The remarks also came days after the Senate rejected a war powers resolution in a 48-51 vote on Nov. 19, leaving Trump's military authority intact.
TRUMP WARNS OF NEW STRIKES AGAINST IRAN AFTER NEW YEAR, CALLS NEGOTIATORS ‘PROFESSIONAL TAP DANCERS’
President Donald Trump monitors U.S. military operations in Iran following an Israeli strike in Tehran on Saturday, Feb. 28, 2026. (@WhiteHouse/X)
Speaking to Fox News earlier Sunday, Trump said he is inclined to resume strikes on Iran after the new year if diplomatic talks fail to produce a deal, warning that Iranian vessels testing the U.S. naval blockade would end up "at the bottom of the sea like the rest of the navy."
In his social media post Sunday, Trump accused both Democrats and Iran of trying to keep fuel prices high ahead of the midterm elections and separately questioned the integrity of the vote without providing evidence.
"Both the Dems and Iran fought like hell to keep the Oil price up as long as possible and, since the Election, the Oil price has dropped by a record level," Trump wrote, adding that it was too bad voters "didn't understand this before they pulled the trigger."

articles.title_orig: Suspected Jewish settler extremist attack Palestinian towns across West Bank
articles.title_zh: Suspected Jewish settler extremist attack Palestinian towns across West Bank
articles.content_orig:
Dozens of militant Israeli settlers raided communities on Saturday night, setting fire to vehicles and several homes
Arson attacks by militant Israeli settlers on Palestinian villages in the occupied West Bank have caused a political row in Israel, drawing condemnation from Gadi Eisenkot, the opposition leader, who described them as “Jewish terrorism”.
Dozens of settlers raided Palestinian communities overnight on Saturday, setting fire to about a dozen vehicles and several homes and scrawling racist graffiti. At least four communities were attacked. Israeli police said they had launched an investigation with forensic teams.
Photographs from Kafr Malik , near Ramallah, showed one slogan written in Hebrew that read: “This is the first revenge.” Several vehicles and homes had been set alight in the village.
Images from nearby Deir al-Sudan showed vehicles on fire. Palestinian reports said an agricultural building had been set ablaze in Deir Ballut and cars torched in Deir Abu Mashal.
An ⁠inconclusive election last month stripped Benjamin Netanyahu, the prime minister, of his majority. Eisenkot has been asked to form a government, though his prospects seem little better.
“Last night’s arson attacks in Judea and Samaria were acts of Jewish terrorism, in every sense of the term,” Eisenkot said, using the biblical name for the West Bank. “Extremist groups that set fire to vehicles and homes are undermining regional stability, putting lives at risk and doing grave damage to Israel’s national security and foreign relations.”
Referring to the far-right ministers Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, he added: “The actions led by Ben-Gvir and Smotrich in the West Bank have brought the area to the brink of unchecked anarchy.”
Eisenkot, who has been given 28 days to form a government by the president, Isaac Herzog, with a possible 14-day extension, urged the government and security establishment to “use every tool at their disposal – including administrative detention and targeted operations by the Shin Bet – to stop the rioters and impose harsh sanctions on them”.
In an unprecedented rebuke on Sunday, several other members of the Israeli parliament criticised Netanyahu over escalating violence by militant settlers against Palestinians.
Yair Lapid, the leader of Yesh Atid, held Netanyahu’s government responsible for encouraging the attacks. “Jewish terrorism is the product of criminal negligence by the Israeli government,” he said on X, adding that ministers were deliberately encouraging the militant settlers’ violence “through their silence”.
Yair Golan, the leader of the Democrats party, warned of the possibility of a third intifada and described the West Bank as “on the brink of an explosion”.
“Anyone who wants to prevent a third intifada must replace the current government, which provides cover and support for Jewish terrorism and abandons security,” Golan said on X. “Jewish terrorism harms innocent Palestinians and Israeli army soldiers, and pushes Israel toward unprecedented international isolation.”
Noam Tibon, a retired army major general and Knesset member, gave a similar warning. “If Israel does not eliminate Jewish terrorism in the West Bank, it will destroy Israel,” he wrote.
Netanyahu has not yet responded to the accusations.
Australia announced sanctions on Wednesday against three people and four Israeli entities, including a construction company, over their role in the expansion of illegal settlements and human rights abuses against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.
A day earlier the UK imposed sanctions on eight Israeli construction companies involved in building illegal settlements in the West Bank, which the UN regards as Palestinian territory under Israeli occupation since 1967.
Since the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attacks on Israel, there has been a surge of Israeli settlement expansion and violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank. More than 1,100 Palestinians have been killed there by Israeli forces or settlers.
On Tuesday, a 72-year-old Palestinian woman was shot dead in an overnight attack by Israeli militant settlers in a village near Jericho, where the group has recently moved in after taking over several Palestinian homes.

articles.title_orig: Finance, fossil fuels and the ‘overshoot’: six key takeaways from Cop31
articles.title_zh: Finance, fossil fuels and the ‘overshoot’: six key takeaways from Cop31
articles.content_orig:
Countries have failed to reach a major new deal to tackle climate change after deep divisions over fossil fuels and money emerged at the UN COP31 talks in Turkey.
Negotiations were due to finish on Friday but ran late into Sunday in search of common ground, becoming the longest UN climate conference in history.
But the final deal proved unacceptable to the EU, Pacific island nations and others because it failed to directly mention fossil fuels, the main cause of global warming.
Meanwhile, many poorer countries objected to the absence of any clear financial commitments from richer nations to help them adapt to the impacts of rising temperatures.
The last time a COP's main political agreement collapsed like this was in 2009 in Copenhagen.
UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres, in his last COP before he steps down, said he was "deeply disappointed".
He took aim at what he called "powerful fossil fuel interests" who he said were taking "a page from Big Tobacco's playbook: distorting the science, delaying policy, blocking action, and piling up huge profits while people everywhere pay the price".
Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, whose country co-hosted the talks, attributed the failure to "difficult geopolitical times".
"That is the reality," he said on Monday.
After two weeks of negotiations, exhausted delegates were presented with a new, draft deal in the early hours of Sunday to try to break the deadlock.
But the words "fossil fuels" did not appear anywhere in the text. The only indirect reference to coal, oil and gas was a nod to a deal agreed at COP28 in 2023 , when countries agreed to "transition away" from fossil fuels in energy systems.
The EU's representative, Irish Minister Darragh O'Brien, made it clear that the EU "strongly" objected, saying that the "decisions go nowhere near the level of ambition needed to tackle climate change".
"It is unconscionable that we would have a climate pact that makes no mention of fossil fuels," he said.
Other countries, such as Panama and the Marshall Islands, also criticised the deal for doing nowhere near enough to tackle the pace of climate change.
A first draft of the deal on Monday mentioned "fossil fuel" or "fossil fuels" six times, but that was unacceptable to oil-producing nations.
Saudi Arabia's delegate Mohammad Ayoub said that Arab countries "continued to engage in good faith" but argued that they only accounted for a small proportion of historical greenhouse gas emissions.
Russia warned not to "turn to slogans" over coal, oil and gas, claiming that if countries moved away from fossil fuels too quickly it would lead to "fuel poverty".
Another major sticking point has been money for poorer countries to adapt to the impacts of climate change, such as more intense heatwaves and more severe droughts.
Last year at COP30 in Brazil , nations agreed to triple the finance for that purpose.
But this year's deal contained no reference to concrete figures, nor the baseline against which that pledge would be measured. This raised fears it would give richer nations too much wriggle room.
"Rich nations and polluting governments cannot keep arriving empty-handed," said Mohamed Adow of Power Shift Africa, an African climate and energy think tank.
The UK's Energy Secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, described the failure to reach a political agreement as "immensely disappointing".
"This only strengthens our resolve to work with partners around the world on the genuine progress made in Antalya on tackling the climate crisis," she said, adding that the UK's commitment was "unwavering".
While talks were hosted in Antalya in Turkey, Australia led the official negotiations - creating what some observers described as a chaotic dynamic.
Chris Bowen, Australian government minister and COP31 president of negotiations, said there were "unbridgeable red lines" in the discussions.
He pointed to "the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory". At the same time, "the impacts of climate change are getting worse", he said, raising the stakes.
The year 2026 could end as the hottest on record and has brought extreme weather and natural hazards to much of the world, from summer heat and drought in Europe to flash flooding in Nepal .
And COP31 was the first annual UN conference to formally discuss how one of the key international targets for limiting climate change would be missed.
In the Paris talks of 2015 , nearly 200 countries agreed to try to limit global warming to 1.5C above pre-industrial levels of the late 1800s, aimed at avoiding some of the worst effects of climate change.
The UN says the Paris deal has driven "near-universal" climate action. In the early 2010s, global warming of 4C or more was thought to be a serious possibility by the end of the century.
Now, the world is likely to limit warming to about 2.8C by 2100 based on current government policies, the UN says.
But action has not been fast enough to meet that Paris goal, with the world likely to "overshoot" 1.5C of long-term warming in the next few years.
Many countries say they are committed to eventually bringing warming back down to 1.5C, but that will require an ambitious ramping up of technologies - which do not yet exist at scale - to remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere.
Although the main deal fell through, some agreements were reached, including progress on a "just transition mechanism" - a framework to support workers and communities as economies shift towards clean energy.
The COP31 president also said more than 80 countries backed Turkey's target to increase the share of global energy use met by electricity to 35% by 2035.
But following the weekend's events, some have questioned whether the UN climate process - which relies on consensus - can succeed in a geopolitically divided world.
The UN's climate chief, Simon Stiell, said he would seek advice on potential reform to the process, with the next conference scheduled for November 2027, COP32 in Ethiopia.
"[The consensus process] has worked to get us where we are," he told the BBC. "It got us through Paris... so it can work," but acknowledged it "fell short" on Sunday.
The UN climate process has "suffered setbacks before and come back stronger," Stiell told delegates. "It must do so again."

articles.title_orig: 'Bottom of the sea': Trump threatens Iranian navy, weighs new attacks by New Year if talks fail
articles.title_zh: 'Bottom of the sea': Trump threatens Iranian navy, weighs new attacks by New Year if talks fail
articles.content_orig:
US President Donald Trump told Fox News on Sunday that he is inclined to resume major military strikes against Iran after the New Year if ongoing negotiations fail to produce an agreement. This signals a possible escalation in the months-long conflict.
In a conversation with Fox News correspondent Trey Yingst, Trump confirmed that indirect talks with Tehran remained underway but expressed deep frustration with Iran’s negotiating tactics.
Describing the Iranians as “professional tap dancers,” Trump accused Tehran of repeatedly engaging in negotiations without making meaningful progress toward an agreement.
“All they do is talk, but it’s all BS,” Trump said.
The president’s comments suggest that Washington is increasingly considering a return to major combat operations if diplomatic efforts fail before the beginning of 2027.
Trump has repeatedly insisted that any agreement with Iran must permanently prevent the Islamic Republic from acquiring nuclear weapons. In an interview with Fox News over the weekend, he said he wanted a deal that would remain effective even under future American administrations.
However, the latest remarks indicate growing doubts about Tehran’s willingness to accept Washington’s terms.
The president also issued a warning to the Islamic regime over reports that Tehran may attempt to challenge the American naval blockade of Iranian ports.
Iranian state media indicated this week that Iranian vessels could seek to test the blockade , which remains in place amid heightened tensions around the Strait of Hormuz.
“I hope they do; they’ll all be at the bottom of the sea like the rest of the navy,” Trump told Fox News, warning of the consequences if Iranian vessels attempt to break through the blockade.
The US president indicated that American forces would open fire on Iranian vessels attempting to violate the blockade.
The warning comes as Iranian attacks against oil tankers continue near the Strait of Hormuz, a critical passage for global energy supplies.
Fox News also reported overnight attacks targeting American forces in Bahrain, highlighting the persistent threat to US personnel and military installations in the region.
Despite extensive American military operations since February 28, when Trump launched Operation Epic Fury, Iran has continued to carry out attacks across the Middle East.
The initial US campaign struck numerous Iranian military targets and killed senior regime officials, dealing significant damage to the country’s military capabilities.
Nevertheless, questions remain about the extent of Iran’s surviving ballistic missile arsenal and its ability to sustain attacks.
According to figures reported by The Wall Street Journal , Iran still possesses approximately 1,500 ballistic missiles and retains the ability to manufacture around 50 additional missiles each month.
Two American aircraft carrier strike groups are currently operating in the Arabian Sea, while US aerial refueling aircraft are positioned in Israel, according to Fox News.
The scope of any renewed American operation remains unclear, and Trump has not announced a final decision to launch additional strikes.
Trump also addressed renewed anti-government protests inside Iran, offering encouragement to demonstrators challenging the Islamic Republic.
The president said he had seen videos of the protests and urged Iranians to continue demonstrating.
The protests come amid growing domestic difficulties, including rolling electricity outages announced by Iranian authorities.
Trump’s remarks add to the pressure on Tehran at a time when the administration is simultaneously pursuing indirect negotiations, maintaining a naval blockade and considering renewed military action.
The president has previously suggested that the Iranian regime may face increasing internal pressure as its economy and military capabilities deteriorate.
Meanwhile, American allies in the Persian Gulf are pressing for a negotiated settlement, fearing that renewed American strikes could trigger another wave of Iranian retaliation against regional energy infrastructure.
During the initial stages of Operation Epic Fury, Gulf countries came under Iranian missile and drone attacks, including strikes targeting energy facilities.
Regional governments remain concerned that another major US offensive could lead Iran to intensify attacks against their territory. An Iranian attack on a civilian industrial facility in Bahrain on Saturday highlighted the continuing threat to Gulf states.
Qatar continues to play a central role in the diplomatic effort, serving as an intermediary and conveying messages between Washington and Tehran in an attempt to reach an agreement.
Trump has acknowledged the importance of Qatar’s involvement in the negotiations.
For now, the United States remains caught between continued diplomatic efforts and the possibility of another major military escalation.
Trump’s latest comments mark a significant warning to Tehran: Unless an agreement is reached, the president is increasingly inclined to return to large-scale military operations after January 1.

articles.title_zh: Court bans China’s BYD from selling ‘Defender clone’ SUV in EU
articles.content_orig:
Reactions to ICJ ruling underline global divisions over court with China raising concerns about judicial overreach
The US has greeted with caution the world’s highest court’s ruling that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, while China has raised concerns of judicial overreach.
Reactions to Thursday’s historic ruling underlined deep international division over the role of the court and similar institutions. The international court of justice (ICJ) had never previously found a state responsible for genocide and the decision could set a precedent for future genocide claims, notably a case against Israel .
The EU hailed a “landmark” judgment from the ICJ, while the UK reaffirmed “full support” for the court and the international legal order. Australia called on Myanmar to comply fully with the judgment and its obligations under international law.
But China, which has offered rare international support for Myanmar’s military rulers since they seized power five years ago, highlighted “issues such as jurisdiction overreach and expanded interpretation”.
“China … believes that such practices are not conducive to the settlement of disputes,” the foreign ministry spokesperson, Guo Jiakun, told a news briefing when asked about the ICJ ruling. “The international community should make joint efforts in this direction to avoid complicating this issue.”
Western nations cut ties with the unstable and poor south-east Asian country after the 2021 coup that ousted a civilian-led government.
Myanmar’s presidential spokesperson said on Friday that the ruling was “unfair”, noting the judges’ nine to six vote. The country’s military rulers have denied carrying out a genocide, claiming their actions targeted a Rohingya militant group that conducted insurgent attacks.
“When we look at the result, not all 15 judges agreed with the decision,” said Khaing Khaing Soe, speaking at a press conference in the capital, Naypyidaw. “So this was not a unanimous decision … I would say it is not fair.”
The US state department said on Thursday that Washington was examining the judgment, while stressing the need to avoid “politicisation” of the ICJ.
Donald Trump’s administration has taken a dim view of international law, vowing to dismantle the international criminal court (ICC), but has yet to question the legitimacy of the ICJ.
The state department reiterated US support for the people of Myanmar and said it shared “grave concerns over the continued abuses of human rights against Rohingya Muslims and members of other minority groups”, noting that the US was the largest single humanitarian donor to the Rohingya humanitarian crisis response.
In Brussels, the EU said Myanmar must fully implement the ICJ’s ruling “without delay” and that “compliance with ICJ’s decisions is not optional, it is an obligation under international law”.
“The European Union holds the ICJ in the highest regard and remains steadfast in its support for its critical role in the peaceful resolution of disputes and the upholding of the rule of law at international level,” an EU spokesperson said in a statement .
“The Rohingya people have endured immense suffering, including displacement and violence, and their plight must not be forgotten. This landmark ruling underscores the imperative of justice for victims and the necessity of upholding international law.”
The UN secretary general, António Guterres, called the ruling “a demonstration of international justice and a reaffirmation that impunity for such horrific acts must not stand”.
The UK expelled Myanmar’s defence attache and called for measures to “ensure the court’s ruling sends a clear message that such crimes cannot be committed with impunity”.
The ruling caps a lengthy legal campaign since August 2017 when Myanmar’s military launched what it called a “clearance campaign” in Rakhine state in response to an attack by a Rohingya insurgent group. Reports rapidly emerged of mass rapes and killings by security forces, as well as the burning of thousands of homes.
Judges rejected Myanmar’s claim that its actions were primarily intended as counter-terrorism operations, or even that they were an attempt to punish or forcibly displace the population but without committing genocide.
The country’s leader, Min Aung Hlaing, who headed the military during the 2016-17 attacks, has a pending arrest warrant from the ICC – which, unlike the ICJ, prosecutes individuals and not states – on allegations of crimes against humanity.
The former general overthrew the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi, triggering a civil war that has left tens of thousands dead. He was installed as civilian president in April after elections that were widely discredited .
While the ICJ does not have the power to enforce rulings, its decisions are considered binding, carry diplomatic weight and can shape international action, including sanctions.
Under the 1948 convention, to establish that genocide occurred the court had to find that there was an intent to destroy the Rohingya “in whole or in part”.
About 1.2 million Rohingya refugees now live in Bangladesh, primarily in crowded camps across the Cox’s Bazar district, where they endure harsh conditions marked by fire hazards, infectious diseases, monsoon landslides, inadequate sanitation and strict work restrictions.
Judges at the court based in The Hague have also been asked to rule on other allegations of genocide.
South Africa has accused Israel of breaching the genocide convention during its offensive in Gaza, a claim Israel vehemently denies. That case is years from completion. An interim ICJ judgment in 2024 ordered Israel to ensure its forces do not commit acts of genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.
Ukraine also has a case pending against Russia . Shortly after Moscow’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, Kyiv accused Russia of fabricating genocide claims against Ukraine to justify the attack.

articles.title_orig: Russia-bound ship towed away after it was attacked in Gulf of Finland
articles.title_zh: Russia-bound ship towed away after it was attacked in Gulf of Finland
articles.content_orig:
A Russian cargo vessel that was hit by a drone attack in the eastern Gulf of Finland is being towed away, authorities have said.
The Sparta II had been bound for Russia's Baltic exclave Kaliningrad when it was hit on Saturday morning, sparking a fire aboard.
It then drifted into Finnish waters and its crew were evacuated to Russia. Finnish defence forces said Ukraine was likely behind the attack. Kyiv has yet to comment.
Finland's Border Guard said on Sunday afternoon that fire was no longer visible from the outside but thermal cameras showed that some containers on the ship were still warm.
The Sparta II was "slightly listing", Finnish authorities added, but the "situation is stable" and no fuel or other "hazardous substance leaks" had been detected.
Kaliningrad Governor Alexei Besprozvannykh said two drones appeared to have been used in the strike and that there was "no threat" to his territory's supplies.
The Sparta II was sanctioned by the US in 2022 and Ukraine earlier this year, and is run by a Russian company, according to the Ukrainian and US governments.
The company says it was established within the structure of Russia's defence ministry in 2011 and since 2015 has been operating within the military construction complex.
Finland's coast guard said it had been alerted to the attack at around 08:50 local time (06:50 GMT) on Saturday and that the cargo vessel had been located approximately 50km west of the island of Suursaari in the Gulf of Finland.
This prompted "temporary aviation and maritime restrictions" around the area, Finnish border officials said.
"War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity," Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said. "Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor."
Shortly after the incident, Finland's defence ministry said a Russian helicopter was suspected of violating the country's airspace, potentially linked to "rescue or tracking operations".
While Besprozvannykh initially said the crew of the Sparta II intended to repair the ship and carry on their journey, the Finnish Border Guard later said they had been evacuated to another Russian vessel that was en route to Russia.
Jukka-Pekka Lumilahti, director of maritime operations at the Finnish Border Guard, said during a news conference on Sunday that one Sparta II crew member had suffered minor injuries.
The Russian rescue vessel Murman is leading towing operations with the support of a Finnish guard ship and a Estonian naval patrol vessel.
Kaliningrad is a Russian exclave that sits between Poland and Lithuania.
Finnish Defence Minister Antti Häkkänen said that the Border Guard was responsible for the investigation into the attack and was co-operating with other relevant authorities.
Nato has also been informed, the defence ministry said.
The Baltic Sea has become a flashpoint in the Russia-Ukraine war, triggered when Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Ukraine has recently ramped up its long-range attacks against Russia beyond the front lines.
Earlier this month, a Ukrainian drone strike hit a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland .

articles.title_orig: Russian cargo ship set ablaze in Baltic Sea drifts into Gulf of Finland
articles.title_zh: Russian cargo ship set ablaze in Baltic Sea drifts into Gulf of Finland
articles.content_orig:
Finland says work is continuing on the Sparta II ship on Sunday
Rescue and firefighting efforts are continuing for a Russian cargo vessel hit by a drone attack in the eastern Gulf of Finland, authorities have said.
The ship - the Sparta II - was bound for Russia's Baltic exclave Kaliningrad when it was hit on Saturday morning, before drifting into Finnish waters. Finnish defence forces said Ukraine was likely behind the attack. Kyiv has yet to comment.
Finland's Border Guard said on Sunday that work was ongoing to make sure the cargo ship did not sink but it was not aware of any danger to surrounding maritime traffic.
Water was still being used to douse the ship on Sunday, and Finland said Estonian and Russian assets were also involved in recovery work.
Kaliningrad Governor Alexei Besprozvannykh said two drones had been used in the strike, based on preliminary information, and there was "no threat" to the territory's supplies.
"War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity," Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said. "Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor."
The Sparta II was sanctioned by the US in 2022 and Ukraine earlier this year, and is run by a Russian company, according to the Ukrainian and US governments.
The company says on its website that it was established within the structure of Russia's defence ministry in 2011 and since 2015 has been operating within the military construction complex.
Finland's coast guard said it had been alerted to the attack at around 08:50 local time (06:50 GMT) on Saturday and that the cargo vessel had been located approximately 50km west of the island of Suursaari in the Gulf of Finland.
This prompted "temporary aviation and maritime restrictions" around the area, Finnish border officials said.
Shortly after the incident, Finland's defence ministry said a Russian helicopter was suspected of violating the country's airspace, potentially linked to "rescue or tracking operations".
A Russian rescue vessel approached the ship and was told by the crew that they did not need to be evacuated, Kaliningrad's governor wrote on Telegram, adding: "The crew is currently carrying out the necessary work and plans to continue on its way."
The Finnish Border Guard later said the crew had been evacuated to another Russian vessel that was now already en route to Russia. The Russian rescue vessel had remained at the location of the stricken ship.
It added that no environmental damage had been detected and that there was no danger to maritime traffic or people.
Kaliningrad is a Russian exclave that sits between Poland and Lithuania.
Defence Minister Antti HÃ¤kkÃ¤nen said that the Finnish Border Guard were responsible for the investigation into the attack and were co-operating with other relevant authorities.
Nato has also been informed, the defence ministry said.
The Baltic Sea has become a flashpoint in the Russia-Ukraine war, triggered when Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Ukraine has recently ramped up its long-range attacks against Russia beyond the front lines.
Earlier this month, a Ukrainian drone strike hit a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland .

articles.title_orig: GTA 6 Glitch Unlocks The FPS On Xbox Series X|S, But With Multiple Drawbacks
articles.title_zh: GTA 6 Glitch Unlocks The FPS On Xbox Series X|S, But With Multiple Drawbacks
articles.content_orig:
If there's anything we could add to GTA 6 as things stand, it'd be an official 60FPS mode. That's obviously not possible right now due to how demanding the game is on PS5 and Xbox Series X|S hardware, even in the case of the PS5 Pro.
Interestingly though, over the weekend, players have discovered the ability to activate what some are calling a "60FPS Glitch" or "60FPS Bug" on Xbox consoles, forcing the game to unlock its FPS and run at a higher frame rate than it's actually supposed to.
Someone called Meowwie64 on Reddit appears to have found this, and here's what they did to activate it:
Now, as mentioned, there are multiple drawbacks here. The first one is that the glitch speeds up most aspects of the game, making it run faster than intended (and look like it's in fast-forward mode!). This is obviously not an ideal way to enjoy GTA 6, and serves as an immediate deal-breaker in my view.
Another one is that reaching 60FPS is pretty much impossible under normal gameplay circumstances. If you're driving down a highway, for example, you're likely only going to get around 35-40FPS at max, with 60FPS and above being saved for situations that require no graphical intensity whatsoever.
And finally, it should be noted that GTA 6 was never intended to be run this way on Xbox Series X|S, and therefore you could run into all sorts of issues - crashes, bugs, maybe even your console overheating. That last one is unlikely, but the game has been specifically built to run at 30FPS on these machines, so it's not worth pushing it in our view.
We'll leave you with some footage of this glitch running on Xbox Series X and Xbox Series S down below (courtesy of the always-excellent Fuzion Xbox Testing ), and prepare for it to be officially fixed in an upcoming GTA 6 update.

articles.title_orig: Delta says ‘automation’ issues causing delays in Atlanta, nationwide
articles.title_zh: Delta says ‘automation’ issues causing delays in Atlanta, nationwide
articles.content_orig:
ATLANTA, Ga. (Atlanta News First) — Delays are mounting across the country for Delta Air Lines flights after a ground stop and ground delay caused by a technical issue, the Atlanta-based airline said.
A ground stop issued Sunday morning for Delta flights on their way to Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport turned into a ground delay, the FAA said Sunday.
The ground delay, which is in effect until at least 1 p.m., means that flights on the ground heading to Atlanta will now be allowed to depart, but they are being delayed nearly an hour.
The ground delays are due to a problem with Delta’s weight and balance automation system, the Atlanta-based airline said.
“Delta teams are using manual workarounds this morning to safely get flights departed while work continues to restore automation,” the airline said.
Because flights are taking longer to depart due to Delta personnel having to manually calculate their weight, it is limiting gate space for arriving flights, exacerbating the delays.
“We are working with our air traffic control counterparts to strategically enact programs to protect airport gates and tarmac areas from congestion at our Atlanta hub,” Delta said.
Delta passengers are reporting delays at multiple US airports online, including Atlanta, Newark, LaGuardia, Reagan National, Dulles, Boston, Baltimore, Miami, Minneapolis, Nashville, San Antonio, Birmingham.
Just before 10 a.m., nearly 500 flights were delayed at the airport, according to FlightAware , a flight tracking website.
The delays come just as the busy Thanksgiving travel period is about to begin. Officials at Hartsfield-Jackson airport expect more than 4 million passengers through Dec. 1, up 5% from last year.
READ: Hartsfield-Jackson airport expects 4 million passengers during Thanksgiving holiday travel
Just days ago, a nationwide ground stop caused mass cancellations at the world’s busiest airport.
Atlanta’s airport General Manager Ricky Smith said the nationwide ground stop told Atlanta News First that the incident was a “big test” as Thanksgiving travel nears.
This is a developing story. Stay with Atlanta News First as we learn more.
Download our Atlanta News First app for your latest news and information.
